[QuantLib](https://www.quantlib.org/) is the most comprehensive open-source library for
quantitative finance. It handles everything from date arithmetic to full term structure
models and derivatives pricing. This post walks through the basics.

## Setup

If you're using the `fineng` conda environment:

```bash
conda install -c conda-forge quantlib-python
```

Then import:

```python
import QuantLib as ql
print(ql.__version__)
```

## Setting the evaluation date

QuantLib has a global evaluation date that anchors all calculations:

```python
today = ql.Date(14, 3, 2026)
ql.Settings.instance().evaluationDate = today
print(f"Evaluation date: {today}")
```

## Building a discount curve

A discount curve maps each future date to a discount factor $P(0, T)$, which represents
the present value of 1 unit of currency received at time $T$.

$$P(0, T) = e^{-r(T) \cdot T}$$

```python
dates = [
    today,
    today + ql.Period(6, ql.Months),
    today + ql.Period(1, ql.Years),
    today + ql.Period(2, ql.Years),
    today + ql.Period(5, ql.Years),
    today + ql.Period(10, ql.Years),
]

discounts = [1.0, 0.978, 0.955, 0.910, 0.820, 0.680]

curve = ql.DiscountCurve(dates, discounts, ql.Actual360())
curve.enableExtrapolation()

# Query the curve
print(f"1Y discount  : {curve.discount(today + ql.Period(1, ql.Years)):.4f}")
print(f"5Y discount  : {curve.discount(today + ql.Period(5, ql.Years)):.4f}")
print(f"10Y zero rate: {curve.zeroRate(10.0, ql.Continuous).rate():.4%}")
```

## What's next

In the next post I'll use this curve to price a vanilla interest rate swap —
computing the fixed rate that makes the NPV zero at inception.
